entries.title: Magic UI
entries.prompt:
# Use Magic UI in a project

Source: Magic UI, https://magicui.design, MIT. Pinned upstream commit `efe76fc5755eca1142dd4f74c1d6f0ace2887e3c`.
Rights: permissive. Install components from upstream and keep the MIT notice.

## Goal

Add one or two animated marketing components to an existing shadcn/ui project without turning the page into a demo reel.

## Use it when

- The page already has shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS variables.
- One section needs a marquee, a text effect, a beam, a globe or a small interaction.
- The team accepts the motion dependency that some components bring.

## Build steps

1. Confirm the project has shadcn/ui initialized and a working Tailwind theme.
2. Pick a component from the vault entry or the component index at `sources/magic-ui/components.md`.
3. Read the component page for its dependencies. Several use Motion or a canvas library.
4. Install one component at a time:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/marquee
   npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/number-ticker
   ```

5. Review the generated file as your own code. Change the defaults, remove unused props, and match the project tokens.
6. Add reduced-motion handling for any continuous animation. The registry does not always include it.
7. Keep the MIT notice in the project. Magic UI is MIT, and the components are copied into your source tree.

## Requirements

- Install only what the page uses. Do not bulk-add the registry.
- Check the bundle impact of canvas and motion dependencies.
- Every component keeps a visible focus state and a reduced-motion path.
- Text effects stay off controls and body copy.
- Components match the project palette instead of shipping the demo colors.

## Do not

- Do not copy the whole registry into the project.
- Do not use the components as the only copy of meaningful content.
- Do not remove the MIT notice.
- Do not present Magic UI components as original work.

## Verify

- `npm run build` passes with no unused dependency warnings.
- Reduced motion stops continuous animations.
- The new section works at 320px and 1440px.
- The license notice is present.

## Attribution

Magic UI, MIT, https://magicui.design. Keep the MIT notice when copying components.
entries.summary: Animated components built on top of shadcn/ui, aimed at marketing pages and landing experiences. Installed from the `@magicui` registry with the shadcn CLI.

entries.title: React Bits
entries.prompt:
# Use React Bits in a project

Source: React Bits by David Haz, https://reactbits.dev, MIT plus the Commons Clause. Pinned upstream commit `e12c22192ac7b4b452c5e2feb9b586d74765d696`.
Rights: restricted. **Do not copy or redistribute the components.** Install them from upstream into the target application only.

## Goal

Use one React Bits component inside an application or product, including a commercial one, without violating the Commons Clause.

## Use it when

- A specific component, such as SplitText, BlurText or a background effect, fits the design.
- The component will live inside your application and will not be sold, sublicensed or redistributed as a component.
- The project can carry the component's dependencies.

## Build steps

1. Choose the language and styling suffix: `JS` or `TS`, then `CSS` or `TW`. For example, `SplitText-TS-TW`.
2. Install from upstream into the target project:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest add @react-bits/SplitText-TS-TW
   ```

   Or:

   ```bash
   npx jsrepo@latest add https://reactbits.dev/r/SplitText-TS-TW
   ```

3. Read the generated file and its dependencies before using it.
4. Adapt it to the project tokens and remove unused options.
5. Keep the React Bits license notice and attribution in the project.
6. Add reduced-motion handling if the component animates continuously.

## Requirements

- The component is used inside an application, website or product.
- The application is not primarily a component library, template marketplace or port collection.
- The component is not resold, sublicensed, bundled as a component pack or republished as a port.
- Accessibility basics are checked: focus, labels, reduced motion, keyboard access.

## Do not

- Do not copy React Bits source out of a public repository and redistribute it.
- Do not include React Bits components in a starter kit, template pack, UI library or npm package that others install.
- Do not sell the components on their own or in a bundle.
- Do not remove the license notice.
- Do not present the components as original work.

## Verify

- The component runs inside the target application.
- The license notice is present.
- Reduced motion stops continuous animation.
- The component works at 320px and 1440px.

## Attribution

React Bits by David Haz, MIT plus the Commons Clause, https://reactbits.dev. Full license: https://github.com/DavidHDev/react-bits/blob/main/LICENSE.md
entries.summary: A large collection of animated React components: text effects, backgrounds, cursor effects, micro-interactions and full components. Installed as source through the shadcn CLI or jsrepo.

entries.title: shadcn/ui
entries.prompt:
# Use shadcn/ui in a project

Source: shadcn/ui, https://ui.shadcn.com, MIT. Pinned upstream commit `96da9cc7f1aa10580a3741664e2a77c721206c00`.
Rights: permissive. Install components as source and keep the MIT notice for substantial portions.

## Goal

Set up shadcn/ui as the primitive layer for a React and Tailwind project, then add only the components the page needs.

## Use it when

- The project is starting and needs accessible primitives with theme tokens.
- The team wants to own and edit component source rather than depend on a runtime library.
- Magic UI or React Bits components will be layered on top.

## Build steps

1. Initialize in a React project with Tailwind and CSS variables:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest init
   ```

2. Add components by name:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest add button dialog card input
   ```

3. Review every generated file like your own code. Replace demo copy, narrow props and match the project tokens.
4. Keep the theme tokens in CSS variables. Do not hard-code colors in component files.
5. Add only the primitives the page uses. Add more when a real screen needs them.
6. Keep the MIT notice for substantial portions copied into the project.

## Requirements

- Focus states, labels, disabled states and keyboard behavior are tested, not assumed.
- Dark and light themes both work through tokens.
- The component files are typechecked and linted like application code.
- Imports use the project alias, not deep relative paths across the app.

## Do not

- Do not treat shadcn/ui as a runtime dependency or a package you upgrade blindly.
- Do not copy every component into the project.
- Do not override accessibility behavior without testing it.
- Do not remove the MIT notice for substantial portions.

## Verify

- `npm run build` passes.
- Keyboard navigation works in dialogs, menus and forms.
- The theme switch changes surfaces through tokens.
- No component file contains hard-coded brand colors.

## Attribution

shadcn/ui, MIT, https://ui.shadcn.com. Keep the MIT notice when copying substantial portions.
entries.summary: The base layer for most of the stack indexed here. Components are copied into your project as source, so you own and edit the files. It is not a runtime dependency.

entries.title: Animated Rocket Shader Hero
entries.source_author: Matthias Hurrle (@atzedent) for the shader; component author not recorded
entries.prompt:
# Build a dark shader hero inspired by Animated Rocket Shader Hero

Source: shader derived from Star Nest by Pablo Roman Andrioli, adapted by Matthias Hurrle (@atzedent). The wrapper author is not recorded. License unknown.
Rights: private-reference. **Do not copy the source.** Write an original shader hero.

## Goal

Build a full-screen dark hero with a slow procedural light field behind the copy. The content must remain readable without WebGL2, and the motion must stop for people who ask for less.

## Use it when

- A landing page needs atmosphere without a hero image.
- The product is technical and a calm, dark first screen fits the tone.
- You can afford a WebGL2 canvas and can keep the copy in HTML.

## Build steps

1. Create a React component with one canvas fixed behind absolutely positioned hero content.
2. Write an original fragment shader. A good starting point is layered value noise or fbm with a slow drift and a soft warm core. Do not derive it from Star Nest or any Shadertoy shader.
3. Add a pointer uniform only if the shader actually uses it. Smoothed pointer influence of a few percent is enough.
4. Compile once, cache the program, and resize to the container with the device pixel ratio capped at 2. Do not multiply the ratio twice.
5. Render one static frame when `prefers-reduced-motion` matches. Pause the loop when the canvas is offscreen or the tab is hidden.
6. Put the copy in real HTML: badge, headline, subtitle, one primary and one secondary action. Keep the canvas `aria-hidden`.
7. Stagger the copy reveal at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 seconds with opacity and translate, and remove it under reduced motion.
8. Provide a CSS gradient fallback for browsers without WebGL2.

## Requirements

- Text contrast stays above 4.5:1 against the darkest and brightest part of the canvas.
- No textures, no per-frame allocations and no more than one draw call.
- The shader is disposed and listeners removed on unmount.
- The hero does not block scroll or keyboard navigation.
- A visible focus ring on both actions.

## Do not

- Do not copy the source component, its shader, its markup or its class names.
- Do not use a Star Nest or Shadertoy derivative. Those carry their own licenses and this one is unknown.
- Do not ship a continuous animation without reduced-motion handling.
- Do not use dynamic Tailwind class names that the compiler cannot see.
- Do not put two default exports in one module.
- Do not claim the visual direction as entirely your own. Credit the inspiration.

## Verify

- The hero renders with WebGL2 disabled and the copy is still readable.
- Reduced motion produces a still frame and no entrance animation.
- The page does not scroll horizontally at 320px.
- The render loop stops when the hero scrolls out of view.

## Attribution

Inspired by Animated Rocket Shader Hero, whose shader derives from Star Nest by Pablo Roman Andrioli and the adaptation credited to Matthias Hurrle (@atzedent). License unknown. No source code was copied.
entries.summary: A full-screen dark hero. A WebGL2 fragment shader paints a drifting cloud and light field, and the marketing content sits above it with staggered fade-ins and warm gradient headings.

entries.title: Animated Shiny Text
entries.prompt:
# Add Animated Shiny Text to a project

Source: Animated Shiny Text by Magic UI, https://magicui.design/docs/components/animated-shiny-text, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and keep the credit.

## Goal

Use one line of text with a slow highlight sweep to signal that something is new. The effect should read as an occasional glint, not a loading state.

## Use it when

- A short release note, status line or announcement needs a little life.
- The line is decorative or secondary, not a control label.
- The surface is clearly light or clearly dark, because the gradient uses black and white stops.

## Build steps

1. Install with `npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/animated-shiny-text`, or copy `AnimatedShinyText.tsx` from the vault entry and keep the MIT notice.
2. Render a single `span`. Pass size, weight and color through `className`.
3. Set `shimmerWidth` between 80 and 140 pixels for a short line. Wider values suit longer text.
4. Keep the default keyframes. They rest for most of the cycle, which is what makes the sweep feel occasional.
5. Add the site-level reduced-motion rule that sets `animation: none` on `.animate-shiny-text`.

## Requirements

- The text is readable at the moment the highlight passes underneath it.
- The line does not wrap in the middle of the effect on small screens. Shorten the copy instead.
- The animation is purely decorative. Set `aria-hidden` when the same message already exists in nearby text.

## Do not

- Do not use it for a button label, form label, error message or anything that must be read while moving.
- Do not run several shiny lines at once. One per view is the point.
- Do not rely on the default `max-w-md` or neutral color. Set them for your surface.
- Do not remove the Magic UI credit or the MIT notice.

## Verify

- Reduced motion shows static text.
- The sweep does not cause a layout shift.
- The line is legible at 320px and at 1440px.

## Attribution

Animated Shiny Text by Magic UI (https://magicui.design), MIT. Keep the MIT notice if you copy it.
entries.summary: A single line of text with a light highlight that sweeps across it. The effect is a clipped background gradient animated with a CSS keyframe, so no canvas or JavaScript animation loop is involved.

entries.title: Dot Pattern
entries.prompt:
# Add Dot Pattern to a project

Source: Dot Pattern by Magic UI, https://magicui.design/docs/components/dot-pattern, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and keep the credit.

## Goal

Add a quiet dot grid behind a section without an image request. The pattern should support the content and never compete with it.

## Use it when

- A section needs texture but not a full background illustration.
- A card or stage needs depth behind a headline or a code sample.
- You want a static texture with an optional glow.

## Build steps

1. Install with `npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/dot-pattern`, or copy `DotPattern.tsx` from the vault entry and keep the MIT notice.
2. Place it inside a positioned container with `relative` and `overflow-hidden`. The SVG is absolute and fills the container.
3. Set spacing with `width` and `height` between 16 and 24. Use `cr` around 1 for a fine grid.
4. Color it with a text utility such as `text-stone-900/10` or `text-white/10`.
5. Mask it with `[mask-image:radial-gradient(...)]` so the grid fades instead of ending at a hard edge.
6. Leave `glow` off for reading sections. Turn it on only for a small, focused panel.

## Requirements

- The SVG stays `aria-hidden` and `pointer-events-none`.
- The dot count stays reasonable. Increase spacing or cap the height on very large sections.
- Glow does not run under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Text over the pattern keeps at least 4.5:1 contrast.

## Do not

- Do not put text directly on an unmasked, full-opacity grid.
- Do not use glow behind long paragraphs.
- Do not rely on container resizes. The component listens to window resize only, so remount it or update spacing when a layout change resizes the parent.
- Do not remove the Magic UI credit or the MIT notice.

## Verify

- The pattern does not intercept clicks or focus.
- The section has no horizontal overflow at 320px.
- Reduced motion removes the glow animation.

## Attribution

Dot Pattern by Magic UI (https://magicui.design), MIT. Keep the MIT notice if you copy it.
entries.summary: A dot grid drawn as SVG circles that fill the parent container. With `glow`, each dot pulses on its own delay. Without it, the pattern is static.

entries.title: Interactive 3D Machine
entries.source_author: Evgeny Shilov (eugeneshilow); built with OpenAI Codex, ported to React by Claude
entries.prompt:
# Build an interactive 3D product machine inspired by Interactive 3D Machine

Source: Interactive 3D Machine by Evgeny Shilov (https://agentic-factory-3d.vercel.app), license unknown.
Rights: private-reference. **Do not copy the source.** Read the public descriptions and write an original scene.

## Goal

Build a React and three.js section where one product is presented as a physical machine with five named stations. The user can orbit the machine, hover and click a station, switch between four levels of detail, and jump between camera presets. The scene must explain the product, not just decorate the page.

## Use it when

- A product has a sequence of five or fewer stages that people keep confusing.
- A static diagram is not enough and a video would be too passive.
- You can afford the three.js bundle and can keep the rest of the page light.

## Build steps

1. Choose the five station names and the one-sentence job of each. Write them down before touching three.js.
2. Scaffold a React component with `react` and `three`. Keep the scene in one module, the controls in another, and the HTML chrome in the component. Do not put the whole thing in one 2,000 line file.
3. Build the machine from primitives: a base plate, five station bodies, connectors, and a few moving parts. Use one environment map for reflections. No downloaded models or images.
4. Add four modes: assembled, cutaway, stations, one order. Each mode changes what is visible and what the camera emphasizes.
5. Add five camera presets: overview, side, top, station and flight. Animate between them with a damped position and target, not a cut.
6. Add raycasting for hover and click. Change the cursor on hover and focus the clicked station. Show the station name in real HTML next to the canvas.
7. Expose a small control object from the component: `setMode`, `setCamera`, `focusStation`, `play`, `pause`. Return it from a ref or an `onReady` callback. Do not attach it to `window`.
8. Add a reduced-motion path that renders a still frame and disables camera flights.
9. Pause rendering when the canvas leaves the viewport or the tab is hidden. Resume on return.

## Requirements

- Canvas has an `aria-label` naming the five stations and the available interactions.
- Every mode and camera control is a real button with `aria-pressed` and a visible focus ring.
- Station names and descriptions exist in HTML, not only in the canvas texture.
- The scene does not trap page scroll. Wheel zoom is disabled unless the user is interacting with the canvas.
- On coarse pointers, allow orbiting or provide explicit rotate buttons. Do not silently disable all rotation.
- Dispose geometries, materials, textures, the environment, the renderer, controls, listeners and observers on unmount.
- Cap the pixel ratio at 2 and keep the machine under roughly 150k triangles.

## Do not

- Do not copy the source, its geometry, its station names or its layout.
- Do not ship a continuously rendering canvas with no visibility check.
- Do not make the canvas the only place where meaning lives.
- Do not use a global `window` object for control.
- Do not claim the original design as yours.

## Verify

- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` shows a still frame and no camera flight.
- Keyboard users can reach every control and read every station name.
- The tab stays near 60fps on a mid-range laptop and does not keep rendering after scrolling away.
- On a phone, the page scrolls normally and the machine remains explorable.

## Attribution

Inspired by Interactive 3D Machine by Evgeny Shilov (https://agentic-factory-3d.vercel.app), license unknown. No source code was copied.
entries.summary: A React and three.js scene of a short-video factory as one physical machine. Five stations sit on a metal plate: engine, admin, storefront, cabinet and cashdesk. You can orbit it, hover a station, click to focus, switch between four modes and jump between five camera presets. Everything is procedural. There are no models, images or textures to download.

entries.title: Liquid Sculpture Hero
entries.prompt:
# Add Liquid Sculpture Hero to a project

Source: Liquid Sculpture Hero by Guglielmo Giannattasio, https://21st.dev/@gughigug/components/liquid-sculpture-hero, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and must keep the visible credit.

## Goal

Build a hero where a single image breaks into roughly one hundred thousand GPU particles and turns liquid under the cursor, then settles back into the image. Without WebGL2 it must show the still image and keep the page usable.

## Use it when

- A portfolio or product hero has one strong image.
- The image can carry the page and the copy is short.
- You can test on a mid-range phone before shipping.

## Build steps

1. Copy `SculptureHero.tsx` from the vault entry, or take it from the 21st.dev component page. Keep the MIT notice and the visible credit link.
2. Pass a local `src` and `mobileSrc`. Do not hotlink the default `cdn.21st.dev` photographs.
3. Set `imageBackground` to the dominant color of your image so the fallback blends in.
4. Leave `height` fluid, for example `clamp(600px, 86svh, 860px)`.
5. Set `loadFonts` to false when your site already loads its own fonts, or self-host the two fonts the component expects.
6. Keep the static image visible until the first canvas frame is ready. Do not hide the fallback on mount.
7. If your host sends no permissive CORS headers, use a same-origin image so `crossOrigin="anonymous"` does not fail.

## Requirements

- The component detects reduced motion and passes it into the engine. Keep that path.
- The canvas is decorative. The image has alt text and the headline is real HTML.
- The layout leaves room between the navigation and the copy at desktop and phone widths.
- Performance is checked on a mid-range phone. Reduce the particle count or use the still image on low-end devices if needed.
- Bundle size is accounted for. Split the component if the rest of the page does not need it.

## Do not

- Do not remove the author credit or the link back to the 21st.dev page. The license and the platform both require it.
- Do not hotlink the sample images.
- Do not ship it without a WebGL2 fallback.
- Do not present the component as your own work.

## Verify

- With WebGL2 blocked, the still image appears and the copy is readable.
- The cursor turns the image liquid and it settles back.
- Reduced motion keeps the image stable.
- The page holds 60fps on a mid-range laptop.

## Attribution

Liquid Sculpture Hero by Guglielmo Giannattasio, MIT, published at https://21st.dev/@gughigug/components/liquid-sculpture-hero. Keep the credit and the license notice.
entries.summary: A hero that rebuilds an image as roughly one hundred thousand GPU particles. The cursor turns the material liquid and it settles back into the crisp image. Without WebGL2 it falls back to a static image.

entries.title: Marquee
entries.prompt:
# Add Marquee to a project

Source: Marquee by Magic UI, https://magicui.design/docs/components/marquee, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and keep the credit.

## Goal

Create a continuous horizontal or vertical strip of cards, labels or logos driven by CSS keyframes, with no JavaScript animation loop.

## Use it when

- A row of principles, logos, testimonials or tags should feel alive.
- The content is decorative or already repeated elsewhere.
- You can keep the motion calm and slow.

## Build steps

1. Install with `npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/marquee`, or copy `Marquee.tsx` from the vault entry and keep the MIT notice.
2. Set `--duration` and `--gap` on the root with arbitrary properties, for example `[--duration:38s] [--gap:1rem]`.
3. Set `repeat` to the number of copies needed to fill the widest viewport. Four is the default.
4. Use `pauseOnHover` for decorative strips, but do not rely on it for keyboard access.
5. Add an edge mask with `[mask-image:linear-gradient(...)]` so items fade rather than cut off.
6. Provide a static, screen-reader-only list of the same content and mark the marquee `aria-hidden`.
7. Keep the Tailwind keyframes for `marquee` and `marquee-vertical` in the theme, and stop them under reduced motion.

## Requirements

- The strip does not cause horizontal page overflow.
- Each item keeps a readable contrast and a consistent width.
- Reduced motion stops the track without hiding the content.
- The strip does not contain a control that keyboard users cannot reach.

## Do not

- Do not put the only copy of meaningful text inside the marquee.
- Do not use hover pause as the only way to stop motion.
- Do not run several marquees in opposite directions in the same view.
- Do not remove the Magic UI credit or the MIT notice.

## Verify

- The page has no horizontal scrollbar.
- Screen readers read the content once.
- Reduced motion shows the items without movement.

## Attribution

Marquee by Magic UI (https://magicui.design), MIT. Keep the MIT notice if you copy it.
entries.summary: A horizontal or vertical marquee that duplicates its children and scrolls them with CSS keyframes. Duration and gap are CSS variables, and the animation can pause on hover.

entries.title: Mascot Portfolio Hero
entries.prompt:
# Add Mascot Portfolio Hero to a project

Source: Mascot Portfolio Hero by Kedhareswer Naidu, https://21st.dev/@kedhareswer/components/mascot-portfolio-hero, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and must keep the visible credit.

## Goal

Build a portfolio hero where a printed poster layout, a generated one-point room and an illustrated character share one screen. The character follows the pointer with layered parallax, blinks, and greets the visitor when clicked.

## Use it when

- A portfolio or studio page can carry a large illustrated character.
- The page has one screen of copy and does not need a scroll to explain itself.
- You can test both a wide desktop frame and a tall phone frame before shipping.

## Build steps

1. Copy `MascotPortfolioHero.tsx` from the vault entry, or install it from the 21st.dev page. Keep the MIT notice and the visible credit.
2. Pass a definite `height` and `minHeight`, for example `height="clamp(560px, 80svh, 780px)"`. Never pass `height="100%"`.
3. Self-host Archivo Black and Inter, or accept the fallback to Arial Black and the system sans. The component names both families in its CSS stacks.
4. Pass `href` on the seeking pill only when it has a real destination. Otherwise leave it out and treat the pill as poster copy.
5. Keep the `aria-label` on the `h1` and the label on the character button. The visible headline letters are decorative and hidden from assistive technology.
6. Test the landscape and portrait layouts at the sizes you will ship. The room and poster depend on container width and height, not on the viewport alone.
7. Keep the pointer loop writing to SVG nodes. Moving the gaze into React state would re-render the poster on every pointer move.

## Requirements

- The hero fits inside its container at both 16:9 and tall portrait shapes.
- The character remains a keyboard-reachable button and the greeting bubble stays polite live text.
- Reduced motion stops the gaze, breathing and blinking while leaving the poster readable.
- The headline is real HTML text, not SVG, and the character illustration has no essential copy inside it.
- The seeking pill is either a real link or non-interactive copy, never a focusable dead control.
- The two display fonts are served from the same origin as the page.

## Do not

- Do not remove the author credit or the MIT notice. The license requires the notice, and this vault requires the credit.
- Do not pass a percentage height. The stage is sized from container height and will collapse.
- Do not put essential copy inside the SVG figure or the decorative room.
- Do not present the component or the character design as your own work.
- Do not add a second copy of the component without checking the duplicated style tag and the global pointer listener.

## Verify

- At a wide desktop size, the headline, services row, seeking pill and character are all visible and do not overlap.
- At a phone size around 390px wide, the portrait layout shows the headline, pill, services and character without horizontal scrolling.
- Moving the pointer turns the head and the eyes follow further than the skull.
- Clicking the character changes the greeting and wiggles the beanie tag.
- Reduced motion leaves a calm poster with no blinking or idle gaze.
- The page has no console errors and the two fonts load from the site origin.

## Attribution

Mascot Portfolio Hero by Kedhareswer Naidu, MIT, published at https://21st.dev/@kedhareswer/components/mascot-portfolio-hero. Keep the credit and the license notice.
entries.summary: A one-screen portfolio hero built as a printed poster for the screen. A one-point-perspective room is generated in SVG, a four-line display headline fills the left, and an illustrated character stands at the right. The head follows the pointer with layered parallax, blinks on its own, and greets the visitor when clicked.

entries.title: Number Ticker
entries.prompt:
# Add Number Ticker to a project

Source: Number Ticker by Magic UI, https://magicui.design/docs/components/number-ticker, MIT.
Rights: permissive. You may copy the published file and keep the credit.

## Goal

Animate a number from a start value to a real target when it scrolls into view, with locale formatting and a spring that settles.

## Use it when

- A stat is already true and worth emphasizing once.
- The number is short enough to read while it animates.
- The section can reserve its final width to avoid layout shift.

## Build steps

1. Install with `npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/number-ticker`, or copy `NumberTicker.tsx` from the vault entry and keep the MIT notice.
2. Pass the real `value`, a sensible `startValue`, and a `delay` between 0 and 0.3 seconds.
3. Use `decimalPlaces` only when the data has decimals. Do not invent precision.
4. Use `direction="down"` when the story is a reduction, such as cost or latency.
5. Reserve width with `tabular-nums` and a `min-width`, so the count does not push the layout.
6. For reduced motion, pass the final value as both `startValue` and `value`. Motion does not detect the preference for you.
7. Keep the label in HTML next to the number, not inside the animated span.

## Requirements

- The number is true at the time of rendering. Do not animate a placeholder.
- The final value is visible without JavaScript.
- The animation runs once when it enters view.
- The label explains the unit and the period.

## Do not

- Do not use it for prices, dates or identifiers.
- Do not stack five tickers in one view.
- Do not remove the Magic UI credit or the MIT notice.

## Verify

- The final value matches the source data.
- Reduced motion shows the final value immediately.
- No layout shift occurs when the count finishes.

## Attribution

Number Ticker by Magic UI (https://magicui.design), MIT. Keep the MIT notice if you copy it.
entries.summary: A number that springs from a start value to a target when it scrolls into view. Formatting uses `Intl.NumberFormat`, so thousands separators and decimals follow the locale rules of `en-US`.

entries.title: Button
entries.prompt:
# Add the UI Vault Button to a project

Source: UI Vault Button by Kone Tshivhinda, MIT, `library/button/`.
Rights: own. Copy the files, keep the MIT attribution line.

## Goal

Add a small, dependency-free React button with four variants, three sizes, a loading state and a visible focus ring. Styling stays in CSS variables so the project can retheme it without editing the component.

## Use it when

- A project needs one good button without a whole component library.
- The design uses CSS variables or a token layer.
- Forms and mobile actions need a reliable `type="button"` default.

## Build steps

1. Copy `Button.tsx` and `button.css` into the project, for example `src/components/button/`.
2. Import the component and render it:

   ```tsx
   import { Button } from "./button/Button";

   <Button variant="primary" size="lg">Start a project</Button>
   <Button variant="secondary" loading>Saving</Button>
   <Button variant="danger" disabled>Delete</Button>
   ```

3. Retheme on the element or a parent with the documented variables:

   ```css
   .my-form .ui-button {
     --ui-button-radius: 8px;
     --ui-button-bg: #0f766e;
     --ui-button-hover: #115e59;
     --ui-button-focus: #0f766e;
   }
   ```

4. Keep the label visible while loading. The spinner sits beside it and `aria-busy` announces the state.
5. Use `type="submit"` explicitly on forms when the button submits.
6. Keep the reduced-motion block that removes the press transform and spinner rotation.

## Requirements

- Focus is only ringed with `:focus-visible`.
- Disabled and loading buttons use the native disabled attribute.
- The label is never replaced by the spinner.
- Button text meets contrast requirements in every variant.
- The component has no runtime dependencies.

## Do not

- Do not use a `div` with an `onClick` instead of the component.
- Do not remove the focus ring or the reduced-motion rules.
- Do not hard-code a new palette in the component. Add a variant or override tokens.
- Do not remove the MIT attribution line.

## Verify

- Tab reaches the button and the focus ring is visible.
- Loading sets `aria-busy` and prevents a second click.
- The button works at 320px with `fullWidth`.
- Reduced motion removes the press transform and spinner rotation.

## Attribution

UI Vault Button by Kone Tshivhinda, MIT. Source: https://github.com/konethegreat/ui-vault/tree/main/library/button
entries.summary: A dependency-free React button with four variants, three sizes, a loading state and a visible focus ring. Styling lives in CSS variables, so a project can retheme it without touching the component.

entries.prompt:
# Add Nebula Hero to a project

Source: Nebula Hero by Kone Tshivhinda, MIT, `library/nebula-hero/`.
Rights: own. Copy the files, keep the MIT attribution and the inspiration credit.

## Goal

Add a WebGL2 hero background made from layered value noise: a slow nebula with a warm core, faint stars and a vignette. Content sits over it with a readable scrim, and the page still works without WebGL2.

## Use it when

- A landing page needs atmosphere without a hero image or video.
- The copy is short and the page can afford one full-screen shader.
- You want a dark hero that stays calm and stops for reduced motion.

## Build steps

1. Copy `NebulaHero.tsx` and `nebula-hero.css` into the project.
2. Render the component with content props:

   ```tsx
   <NebulaHero
     eyebrow="UI Vault"
     headline="Interfaces with gravity."
     body="A short supporting line."
     primaryCta={{ label: "Browse the catalog", href: "#catalog" }}
     secondaryCta={{ label: "Read the code", href: "#source" }}
     height="min(88svh, 780px)"
   />
   ```

3. Replace the default CTAs and credit text with the project's real links.
4. Keep the pointer influence subtle. It shifts the noise field by a few percent.
5. Keep the reduced-motion branch that renders one static frame.
6. Keep the offscreen and visibility checks that pause the loop.
7. Keep the CSS radial gradient so the hero still has depth without WebGL2.

## Requirements

- The canvas is `aria-hidden` and all content lives in HTML.
- Text contrast stays above 4.5:1 over the brightest part of the shader.
- The device pixel ratio is capped at 2.
- There are no textures and no per-frame allocations.
- The shader is deleted and listeners removed on unmount.

## Do not

- Do not remove the reduced-motion branch or the visibility pause.
- Do not put long paragraphs over the busiest part of the shader.
- Do not remove the Star Nest and Matthias Hurrle inspiration credit from the component or the project.
- Do not present the shader as derived from their code. It is a clean-room implementation.

## Verify

- With WebGL2 blocked, the gradient and content still render.
- Reduced motion produces a still frame.
- The loop stops when the hero is offscreen.
- The hero has no horizontal overflow at 320px.

## Attribution

Nebula Hero by Kone Tshivhinda, MIT. Visual direction inspired by Star Nest by Pablo Roman Andrioli (https://www.shadertoy.com/view/XlfGRj) and the shader adaptation credited to Matthias Hurrle (@atzedent). No shader code was copied.
entries.summary: A WebGL2 hero background made from layered value noise: a slow nebula with a warm core, faint stars and a vignette. Content sits over it with a readable scrim. All code is original and MIT.
